claims.claim: Morality and religion have been closely intertwined in Western thought from the beginnings of the Abrahamic faiths and of Greek philosophy, and the separation of morality from religion is comparatively recent; moral vocabularies still carry that history.

Religious traditions generate moral guidance through multiple channels, including scripture and its interpretation, inherited tradition, reason, revelation or religious experience, and community deliberation.

Scripture functions through interpretation: the Talmud is described in OpenStax's survey as a collection of sacred Jewish oral interpretation of the Torah, and interpreters within a tradition can disagree about a text's meaning.

Reason operates alongside scripture and tradition within religious ethics: Thomas Aquinas described natural law as human participation in eternal law through practical reason, and some Islamic theologians held that right and wrong are known by reason independently of revelation, while others located the standard in God's command.

Revelation is understood in some traditions as a channel of moral knowledge: the Qur'an is described as given to Muhammad, whose teachings and practices explained and reinforced it, and John Locke held that moral obligation is known from revelation.
Religion is a social institution: an organized, integrated set of beliefs, behaviors, and norms centered on social needs and values, usually practiced in a public way by a group.

Comparative survey finds recurring moral emphases across traditions, expressed in each tradition's own idiom: compassion and moderation in Taoist teaching; jen, the kind treatment of every person, in Confucian thought; the moral life and acceptance of others in Buddhism; moral behavior and action in Judaism; and charity (caritas), treating others as one would like to be treated, in Christianity.

Care for others and for outsiders appears in Jewish and Christian scripture: Jesus is described as summing up the commandments as love of God and love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18), and the parable of the Good Samaritan presents an outsider as the model of neighborly care.
Justice and care for the weak appear in the Hebrew Bible's depiction of God as a ruler who gives life-giving laws, defends the innocent, and cares for the weak.
Honesty is part of the obligations to other people in the second table of the Ten Commandments, which prohibits killing, adultery, stealing, lying, and coveting.

Stewardship of creation is a contested religious reading of human relations with nature: John Passmore argued that the Judeo-Christian tradition contains resources for regarding humans as stewards of God's creation, while Lynn White's influential thesis read the same tradition as despotic toward nature.

Casuistry is the application of general moral principles to definite and concrete cases of human activity; it presupposes moral principles and applies them to particular situations, and although abuses of the method have drawn criticism, its defenders treat it as a necessary part of moral reasoning.

Religious ethics and philosophical ethics differ in their foundations: religious moral reflection characteristically draws on revelation, scripture, and tradition alongside reason, while philosophical ethics seeks to ground moral claims in reason alone; the two projects are distinct though historically intertwined.

Religious traditions are internally diverse: interpretive communities may disagree on moral and interpretive questions (for example, New Testament scholars disagree about the extent to which Jesus claimed to be God, and medieval Sunni ethical theory divided between Mu'tazilite rationalism and Ash'arite voluntarism), so a tradition does not speak with one voice.

Ritual obligations and moral obligations can stand together in a single inherited framework: the first table of the Ten Commandments concerns obligations toward God directly, including worship and the Sabbath, while the second table concerns obligations toward other people.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the Judeo-Christian tradition relates to nature: stewardship versus domination.
positions: Passmore argued the tradition contains resources for regarding humans as stewards or perfectors of God's creation.
Lynn White's influential thesis read the same tradition as despotic toward nature.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents stewardship of creation as one contested religious reading, not as a universal or settled teaching, and notes that traditions interpret such themes differently.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether reason or revelation grounds moral knowledge within religious traditions.
positions: Mu'tazilite theologians held that right and wrong are known to human reason independently of revelation.
Ash'arite theologians held that God's command sets the standard of right and wrong; Locke similarly grounded obligation in revelation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes both positions neutrally as positions within and across traditions, adjudicating neither, and uses the contrast to illustrate internal diversity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The standing of casuistry as a method.
positions: Casuistry has been criticized historically, with errors and abuses accompanying its practice (the word is sometimes used dismissively).
Defenders treat casuistry as a necessary application of general principles to concrete cases, 'as old as human conscience.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the neutral methodological sense (applying principles to cases) and notes the criticism descriptively without endorsing either evaluation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether recurring moral themes across traditions amount to a universal ethic.
positions: Comparable emphases (compassion, justice, honesty, care for outsiders) appear across many traditions.
Traditions express, prioritize, and interpret these themes differently, and some readings are contested.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes these as common themes, explicitly not universal rules, and keeps the comparative frame descriptive.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('Ethics is a foundational concept in Religious Studies. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') contained no verifiable disciplinary content and was discarded.
The generated draft treated ethics as a generic study skill rather than as the scholarly field of religious ethics.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a descriptive account of religious ethics as a comparative scholarly field.
Added the five channels of moral guidance (scripture and its interpretation, tradition, reason, religious experience, community deliberation), each named and evidenced.
Added comparative treatment of common moral themes, explicitly framed as common themes rather than universal rules.
Added the religious-ethics versus philosophical-ethics distinction, stated neutrally, with normative moral theory scoped to the philosophy subject.
Added descriptive, neutral treatment of religious disagreement and internal diversity.
Added source-backed questions with four options each and varied cognitive demands.
rightsIssues: The Britannica article 'religious ethics' was attempted (live site and Internet Archive) but was blocked by Cloudflare and has no archived capture; it was not used. Substituted scholarly reference sources (SEP) and OER survey material (OpenStax).

All five used sources were employed for fact-checking and synthesis only; no source prose was reproduced beyond ordinary disciplinary terms. The 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia text is public domain, but its New Advent presentation is a modern site, so it is treated as reference-only.
No individualized moral advice is given; examples are neutral and hypothetical.

sourceRecords.title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live entry (first published 2006; substantive revision 2024) via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports the historical intertwining of morality and religion in Western thought; the channels of moral guidance (scripture and God's command in the Hebrew Bible and New Testament, rabbinic law and interpretation, Aquinas on natural law and practical reason, revelation for Locke, Mu'tazilite versus Ash'arite positions in Islam); love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) and the Good Samaritan; justice themes in the Hebrew Bible; the second table of the Ten Commandments; and the modern separation of philosophical ethics (deists, Kant). Copyrighted reference; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Casuistry — The Catholic Encyclopedia (1913)
sourceRecords.provider: New Advent (Knight Foundation / public-domain 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live New Advent page via curl. Supports the definitional account of casuistry as the application of general moral principles to definite and concrete cases, its presupposition of moral principles, the historical objection to abuses of the method, and the defense that some form of case application is a necessary part of moral reasoning. The 1913 text is public domain; the site presentation is modern, so the source is used reference-only and no wording is reproduced. The lesson generalizes the method comparatively rather than confining it to Catholic moral theology.
